q-81506:
The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{6}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\frac{\pi }{6})=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3+{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})]}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =3+([\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{6})]-[\operatorname{sin}⁡(0-\frac{\pi }{6})]) \\  & =3+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =3+(0-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

q-120998:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=0.5$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0.5,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(0.5)+{\int }_{0.5}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & ={e}^{2}+{\int }_{0.5}^{2}{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{2}+{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t+1}]}_{0.5}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(2)+1}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(0.5)+1}) \\  & ={e}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{5}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}+{e}^{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=\frac{{e}^{2}+{e}^{5}}{2}.$

q-81509:
The position of the particle at $t=6$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,6].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(6)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(0)=-2$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=0$ to $t=6.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=9.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=-2+9=7
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=7.$

q-18227:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,0) & 0 & (0,2) & 2 & (2,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ on the interval $(0,2).$

q-73443:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,0) & 0 & (0,3) & 3 & (3,\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the interval $(0,3).$

q-132666:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6)<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to

$$
4x-6<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-6 & <0 \\ 4x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,\frac{3}{2}).$

q-132667:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 4x \\  & =\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1}<0.
$$

The function $2{x}^{2}+1$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
4x<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

q-48860:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x)$ using the product  rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}\cdot x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1>0.
$$

Solving $\operatorname{ln}⁡x=-1$ gives the critical point

$$
x={e}^{-1}\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{e}.
$$

From the graph, we see that this critical point is a minimum. We also see that the slope of the tangent lines is negative to the left of the critical point and positive to the right of the critical point. 

So, we summarize the sign of the derivative in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{1}{e}) & \frac{1}{e} & (\frac{1}{e},\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval $(\frac{1}{e},\infty ).$

q-49006:
From the graph, we see that

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-2$ is negative, so ${f}^{′}(-2)<0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is positive, so ${f}^{′}(-1)>0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is zero, so ${f}^{′}(1)=0.$

Therefore , ${f}^{′}(-2)<{f}^{′}(1)<{f}^{′}(-1).$

q-114698:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31402:
Let $u={log}_{5}⁡(3x).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{x{log}_{5}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{{log}_{5}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡5\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡5\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{5}⁡(3x)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-73655:
Let $u={log}_{4}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $4$ | $16$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{16}\frac{2}{x{log}_{4}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{log}_{4}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡4\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡4{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|){|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡4\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =4{ln}^{2}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

q-79425:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{y}^{3} & =4x \\ 3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x(2+{y}^{3}) \\ \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=2+{y}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{2+{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2} & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3}) & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}} \\ 2+{y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{3} & =K{e}^{{0}^{2}}-2 \\ 1 & =K-2 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}=3{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2.
$$

q-31412:
If we let $u=-x$, then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {5}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {5}^{u}\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int {5}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =-\frac{{5}^{-x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-141738:
The concavity of a function refers to the direction in which its graph curves.

- If the graph curves upward, like a "smile" ($⌣$), then the graph is said to be *concave up*.

- If the graph curves downward, like a "frown" ($⌢$), then the graph is said to be *concave down*.

It's helpful to remember the mnemonic "concave down like a frown."

Only graph II curves upward (like a "smile") among the given graphs.
